raw_response:
I am getting old, so I will not spread myself too thin this year. On 12 mu, I will keep the steady way that has fed us for years: most land in wheat-maize rotation, and a smaller piece in cotton. Wheat and maize are still the safest for me. Cotton can bring cash, but it needs more hand work, and with only two people in the house I cannot manage too much of it. So I plan to keep about 8 mu in wheat followed by summer maize, and 4 mu in cotton.

For wheat, I will sow in early October like we usually do in Quzhou. I have farmed this land a long time, and if wheat misses the right window, it affects tillering and next summer's maize too. I usually use improved local seed, not the most expensive kind, and I put a good share of fertilizer as base fertilizer before sowing. The extension fellow said not to push nitrogen too hard, but in my experience if wheat looks weak after winter, you cannot recover the yield easily, so I still leave enough for a topdress at jointing. I have well water, but pumping costs money, so I will irrigate around three times for wheat, mainly at sowing if dry, at jointing, and at grain filling if spring stays dry. After wheat harvest in June, I will plant maize quickly on the same 8 mu. That turnaround is always tight, so I will keep tillage simple and use rotary tillage or direct sowing if I can hire the machine in time. For maize, I will not overdo fertilizer, because wheat already used a lot and cash is tight, but I still need enough base fertilizer and one topdress around big flare stage. If summer rain is normal, maybe I irrigate once or not at all; if it turns dry, I will use the well once or twice.

Cotton is different. It gives cash, but it takes labor for management and picking. At my age I cannot expand it. I will keep only 4 mu, use a familiar hybrid seed that neighbors also plant, and manage fertilizer in two to three splits so the plants do not grow too wild early. Cotton does not need as much water as wheat in my way of farming, but I will irrigate once or twice if the stand is poor or flowering meets dry weather. For pests, I watch the field first. If aphids or bollworms show up, then I spray. I do not spray just for nothing because every bottle costs money. Overall, I would rather stay with what worked last year than gamble on some new practice.
